task_context.problem_statement: Jordan wants to divide his $\frac{48}{5}$ pounds of chocolate into $4$ piles of equal weight.  If he gives one of these piles to his friend Shaina, how many pounds of chocolate will Shaina get?
task_context.reference_solution: We need to divide the amount of chocolate Jordan has by the the number of piles, so our expression is $\frac{48}{5} \div 4$.  Recall that dividing is the same as multiplying by the reciprocal.  Therefore, $\frac{48}{5} \div 4$ is the same thing as $\frac{48}{5} \cdot \frac{1}{4}.$ We can rewrite $\frac{48}{5} \cdot \frac{1}{4}$ as $\frac{1}{5} \cdot 48 \cdot \frac{1}{4}$, or $\frac{1}{5} \cdot \frac{48}{4}$. To simplify this, divide $48$ by $4$, which equals $12$. Our previous expression, $\frac{1}{5} \cdot \frac{48}{4}$, then equals $\frac{1}{5} \cdot 12$, which comes to $\frac{12}{5}$.  So Shaina will receive $\boxed{\frac{12}{5}}$ pounds of chocolate.

I'll multiply the numerators and the denominators. $48 \times 1 = 48$ and $5 \times 4 = 20$. So I get $\frac{48}{20}$.
